options.explanation: Traffic collisions ✓ — means collisions involving vehicles or road users in traffic; it is neutral and common in safety reporting. Here, road-safety context favours the neutral collision framing. That wording is natural for this precise type of road-safety event, so Traffic collisions is the best answer.

Road crashes — means crashes occurring on roads and is common in road-safety language. This is a strong alternative when the context is broad road-safety reporting, but it misses the narrower vehicle, formal, or terminology distinction tested here. The decisive clue is that road-safety context favours the neutral collision framing.

Traffic accidents — means accidents occurring in traffic and is common in everyday and general reporting. This is common, but it uses the broader accident framing rather than the collision/crash terminology required by the clue. The decisive clue is that road-safety context favours the neutral collision framing.

Traffic incident — is broader and can include breakdowns, obstructions or congestion without any crash. This is too broad: an incident may be a breakdown, obstruction or traffic-management problem with no collision at all. The decisive clue is that road-safety context favours the neutral collision framing.

Near miss — means a dangerous event in which a crash almost happened but did not. This is factually different because no actual crash or collision occurs. The decisive clue is that road-safety context favours the neutral collision framing.

Breakdown — means a mechanical failure of a vehicle rather than a collision. This is a vehicle malfunction, not a collision event. The decisive clue is that road-safety context favours the neutral collision framing.
